title: mini-quarantine-probe-zheng
body:
Purpose:
Quick, small-scale experiment to exercise host-quarantine / routing fallback behavior and measure p99+ latency amplification when one node in a 6-node serving pool is artificially throttled (quarantined) but still accepting some requests. Goal is to surface how much end-to-end latency and error-rate exposure the router and cache layers introduce before traffic fully drains to healthy nodes.

Why this is different from other surge/warmup notes: most previous scratchpads focus on bursty ingress or warm-cache dynamics across the whole fleet. This probe intentionally isolates a single node misbehaving (CPU contention + simulated networking slowness) to replicate a class of flaky-host failures we saw in ENG-5421. The pattern tends to produce long tails and sporadic 5xxs because partial KV-cache hits still route to the quarantined host.

Environment (mini local cluster):
- cluster: 6 identical serving instances (g4dn-like config) behind router v2 (rolling canary of router prioritization).
- model: rwinf-mira-7b-q4a (quantized, KV-cache enabled).
- runtime: serving-runtime@main#b27f (includes latest backpressure heuristics).
- generator: custom python harness (scripts/perf/quarantine_probe.py) using asyncio + httpx, ramp schedule built-in.
- metrics: Prom + Grafana (latency histograms, qps, errors), router traces (sampled), and per-host request counters.
- seed prompt: 32 tokens average, deterministic small prompt set (dev-lab-probeset-32.txt).

Test plan (single run takes ~25m):
1) Warm caches: 15m sustained QPS=40 to get KV cache warmness ~85% across hosts.
2) Stabilize for 5m at QPS=40. Capture baseline percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999).
3) Introduce quarantine on host-3: two changes applied simultaneously:
   - tc netem: add 120ms latency + 20ms jitter on eth0 on host-3 (simulate network slowness)
   - cgroup: limit cpu to 35% of 1 core on serving process (simulate CPU contention)
   note: do not remove host from pool; keep it healthy in control plane to test edge routing decisions.
4) After quarantine, continue QPS=40 for 10m and capture telemetry. Also force a 10% ramp to QPS=44 for 2m to observe elasticity.
5) Remove quarantine and observe recovery for 5m.

Key metrics captured (selected):
- baseline (pre-quarantine, 5m window): p50=31ms, p90=57ms, p95=73ms, p99=112ms, p999=281ms, qps=40, errors=0.
- during quarantine (window 4-9m after injection): p50=33ms, p90=68ms, p95=97ms, p99=360ms, p999=1.2s, qps=39.8, errors=0.6% (502/504 from host-3 proxies).
- ramp-peak (QPS=44): p99=520ms, p999~1.4s, errors rose to 1.9% (mainly 504 gateway, timeouts from router retries).
- recovery (5m after removal): percentiles return toward baseline within ~110s, p99 ~150ms then to ~120ms at 5m.

Ascii latency sketch (p99 window comparison, rough):
- baseline: |====| (112ms)
- quarantine: |============| (360ms)
- ramp: |==================| (520ms)
- recover: |======| (150ms)

Observations / hypotheses: 
- Router retains the quarantined host as "usable" for about 20-40s after first high-latency request; during that time a non-trivial fraction (~8-12%) of requests still land on host-3 depending on routing seed. That explains the initial p99 spike.
- KV-cache interaction: host-3 had higher local cache hit rate for a subset of prefixes (~6%), so the router attempted sticky-ish routing for those prefixes; when host-3 slowed, those prefixes experienced amplified tail because of cache affinity.
- Retries: router-level retries are conservative (single retry) and often retry to the same host because of sticky hashing. This produced extra client-visible latency rather than immediate failover.
- Error profile: most errors were 504s (router timeouts) and a small fraction of 502s from the runtime process crash-looping under CPU cap.
- Recovery: once quarantine removed, cluster-level metrics show smoothing over ~2 minutes; cache priming mostly intact so steady-state recovered faster than a full cold-warmup.

Quick tracing notes (samples):
- trace #A (slow request): router->host-3 forward 160ms wait, runtime exec 220ms, kvcache lookup 18ms, total 410ms, no retry.
- trace #B (retry): router timeout @300ms -> retry -> host-5 served in 42ms -> total client latency 350ms (wasted wait on first attempt).

Immediate takeaways / mitigations to try next: 
1) Lower router sticky affinity window for Hash-based routing (experiment: reduce affinity TTL from 30s to 5s) to avoid repeated attempts to a quarantined host for cache-local prefixes.
2) Introduce faster failure detection: add an active latency sampling probe per-host in router that marks host as soft-evict after N latency samples > 4x median.
3) Make router retry target selection prefer different host (not same hash) when retrying after remote latency exceeds threshold.
4) On the runtime side, expose a lightweight /health-latency endpoint that returns p95 observed CPU-queue latency for quick decisions by router.
5) Add metrics to observe "sticky cache fraction" (fraction of requests that are cache-local to a single host) so we can quantify risk of single-host slowdowns.

Follow-ups / TODOs (ordered):
- [ ] Re-run with affinity TTL=5s (short-run) and compare p99. Owner: Zheng. ETA: 2026-03-05. (blocked: need config flag in router; see PR #781 linked).
- [ ] Create small canary (2 hosts) where one host gets netem latency synthesized every 2m to validate soft-evict heuristic. Owner: Marta. ETA: 2026-03-11.
- [ ] Add a Grafana panel: "sticky_cache_fraction" and correlate with p99. Owner: Devops. ETA: 2026-03-15.
- [ ] File Tech Debt: router should prefer alternate host on retry; add RFC. Owner: Zheng. ETA: 2026-03-20. Linked: JIRA-ENG-5421.

Notes to self (quick):
- This mini run is lightweight and reproducible in lab; scripts/perf/quarantine_probe.py has blocks for tc/cgroups toggles.
- Watch out for test contamination: when applying cgroups, ensure the host's exporter doesn't die (it happened once and produced misleading zero-CPU metrics).
- For the next run capture per-prefix routing distribution to quantify how many prefixes are >50% served by quarantined host.

Raw sample logs excerpt (sanitized):
[2026-02-28T14:12:32Z] router: req id=aa21 -> host-3 forward 0.160s
[2026-02-28T14:12:32Z] host-3 runtime: exec req id=aa21 cpu-queue=0.218s model-exec=0.190s
[2026-02-28T14:12:32Z] router: req id=aa24 -> host-3 forward 0.310s -> timeout -> retry host-5 -> success 0.045s

Final quick conclusion:
Single-host quarantines that keep the node in the routing pool can produce large p99/p999 amplification because of cache affinity + sticky routing + conservative retry policies. Short-term mitigations (affinity TTL reduction and smarter retry targets) yield most of the benefit quickly and are low-risk to roll.

If useful we can convert this into a short playbook and an automated mini-canary that runs on deploys that touch routing code. For now mark as draft and iterate on the reduced-affinity experiment next.

-- Zheng
